amendments.rule: Reserve `noncompositional` for a genuinely indivisible phrase. Both heads are required and must belong to their respective arrays. Use the lexical English anchor as target head; where the source phrase has no uniquely defensible internal head, use its first source token as the deterministic display anchor rather than leaving the head null. **But read rules 23 and 30 before reaching for that fallback.** Where the fused expression's single English word writes one morpheme's own lexeme, that morpheme is the uniquely defensible head and the fallback does not reach it: `בְּעֵינֵי פַרְעֹה` → *Pharaoh* heads on the name and `בְעֵינֵי עֲבָדָיו` → *servants* on the noun, exactly as rule 30 heads a fused expression on the morpheme carrying the lexeme and rule 23 heads a preposition fused with its construct noun on the construct. What the fallback governs is a phrase whose one English rendering writes no morpheme's lexeme in particular — an idiom rendered by a word of its own, or a compound of function morphemes — and not one where a name or noun standing in the phrase is the very word the ASV wrote. Where the rendering runs to several English words and more than one morpheme's lexeme is written among them, no single morpheme is uniquely defensible on that ground and the fallback stands, as it does for `יִּתֵּן קֹלוֹ בִּבְכִי` → *he wept aloud*.
amendments.why: GEN.45.16 sent two one-word fusions to the first-token fallback although the English word written was the name Pharaoh and the noun servants, while the same chapter headed its other fusions on the lexeme-bearing morpheme. The fallback's condition, no uniquely defensible internal head, was being read as satisfied whenever the phrase was fused at all, which quietly overrides rules 23 and 30. The added sentences narrow it and keep the genuine fallback case, GEN.45.2's five-morpheme idiom, working as before.

amendments.rule: A verbless clause supplies its English copula from the construction, not from nothing. In *that it was good*, the supplied *it was* belongs to the unit headed on `טוֹב`; do not mark it `added`. **Where the ASV renders a verbless clause with a presentative *there was* or *there were*, the dummy *there* is part of the same construction-supplied frame as the copula and joins the unit that bears that copula under this rule.** It is never `added`, and the unit still heads on its lexical predicate or anchor. **The anchor may be of any kind, since what licenses the dummy is the presentative frame the construction supplies and not the part of speech the frame is built on.** A nominal anchor, a prepositional predicate and an adverbial anchor are read alike: `וְעוֹד חָמֵשְׁ שָׁנִים` → *and* ***there are yet*** *five years* gives *there are yet* to `עוֹד`, headed on *yet*, and the numeral phrase keeps its own English. Do not read the list as closed and mark the dummy `added` because the anchor is neither a noun nor a preposition; the sentence above says it is never `added`, and rule 17 puts the same dummy on a finite verb and rule 50 on an existential `אַיִן`. **But the dummy this sentence governs is the presentative *there* and no other.** A cleft or impersonal *it* the ASV writes in such a clause — *it was not you that sent me hither*, *It is enough* — is not a presentative frame and no morpheme licenses it, so it is its own `added` unit under rule 30, exactly as the supplied lexical verb of the next sentence is. **Apart from that presentative dummy, this covers the copula and nothing more.** Where the ASV instead supplies a whole *lexical* verb for a clause whose Hebrew has none — the allotment formula `וְלִבְנֵי קְהָת הַנּוֹתָרִים ... עָרִים עָשֶׂר` → *And unto the rest of the sons of Kohath* ***were given*** *by lot ... ten cities* — no morpheme's rendering that verb completes, and it is `added` under rule 30, together with any object the ASV supplies alongside it, as in *were given them*. Test by asking which morpheme is there to carry the English: `הָיָה` carries the *have* of rule 43 and the frame of rule 21, a Hebrew verb carries the light verb of rule 44, and a preposition that is itself the predicate carries the copula of rule 49 — but a preposition the ASV has already spent a word on, as in *unto the rest*, carries nothing further, and a clause with no verb in it at all licenses no verb. **The same lexical-verb boundary holds inside a nominal recasting.** A construct relation can license the English preposition used for it, but not a supplied lexical participle: `חֲמַס אֶרֶץ` → *violence done to the land* gives *violence* to the construct noun and *to the land* to its dependent under rule 19, while *done* is `added` because no source verb licenses it. This is not rule 31's generic completion of a substantive's lexeme: *done* predicates an event of the violence rather than naming the violence. **The copula goes to the predicate, and where a predicate morpheme is present an explicit subject takes only its own English.** Where the clause writes its subject — a pronoun such as `אָנֹכִי`, `אֲנִי`, `אַתְּ` or `הוּא`, or a subject noun — that morpheme takes the English pronoun or noun realizing it and nothing more, while the supplied *am*, *art*, *is*, *are* or *was* joins the predicate, exactly as rule 49 puts it on the preposition heading a prepositional predicate and rule 34 puts it on the predicate a gapped line licenses. `עֶבֶד אַבְרָהָם אָנֹכִי` → *I* ***am*** *Abraham's servant* gives *am* to `עֶבֶד` and *I* to `אָנֹכִי`; `בַת מִי אַתְּ` → *Whose daughter* ***art*** *thou* gives *art* to `בַת`; `הוּא אֲדֹנִי` → *It* ***is*** *my master* gives *is* to `אֲדֹנִי`; and `מִי הָאִישׁ הַלָּזֶה` → *What man* ***is*** *this* gives *is* to `מִי`, which is the clause's predicate, leaving *this* to the demonstrative. **A tripartite clause whose resuming pronoun the ASV renders by nothing but that copula is read on those same terms.** Where the clause writes a subject noun and resumes it with `הוּא`, `הִיא` or `הֵמָּה` before the predicate, and the ASV realizes the subject once by the noun, the resuming pronoun is the unrendered occurrence and is its own `unrepresented` unit under rule 22, while the copula joins the predicate as the preceding sentences direct, discontinuous around a possessive or an article under rule 25: `יְהוָה הוּא נַחֲלָתוֹ` → *Jehovah* ***is*** *their* ***inheritance*** gives *is inheritance* to `נַחֲלָה` and leaves `הוּא` nothing. Do not give the copula to that pronoun on the ground that a present morpheme takes its English before a construction-supplied reading: what that reasoning governs, in rules 46, 47 and 48, is an English word some morpheme's own sense answers to, and a copula answers to the predication rather than to the pronoun, which is why this rule sends it to the predicate wherever a predicate morpheme stands. Where instead the ASV writes a word of its own for the pronoun — `הוּא הַדָּבָר` → ***that*** *is the thing* — that pronoun is holding an English word already and is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw, and the copula still joins the predicate. One chapter may write both shapes, and DEU.18.2 and DEU.18.22 do. **Where the predicate is wholly elided and no predicate morpheme is available to bear the construction-supplied copula, the copula instead joins the explicit subject as the clause's sole overt anchor:** `אֲנִי` → *I am*. This exception does not apply where a predicate is written. **And a copula the ASV fronts as a question auxiliary belongs to the interrogative particle, not to the predicate.** Where `הֲ`, or the `אִם` opening a following disjunctive question, stands in a verbless clause and the ASV writes a single *Is*, *Am*, *Art*, *Are* or *Was* at the clause head, that one word is both this rule's construction-supplied copula and the question auxiliary rule 17 gives the particle: the particle takes it and heads on it, and the predicate keeps only its own English. `הֲלֹא יִרְאָתְךָ כִּסְלָתֶךָ` → ***Is*** *not thy fear of God thy confidence* gives *Is* to `הֲ` and leaves `כִּסְלָה` the bare *confidence*. This is rule 50's reading of an interrogative existential clause holding for a verbless clause with any predicate, and rule 17's *belongs to the interrogative particle and not to the verb* holding where there is no verb to compete for the word. Where the ASV writes a second copula for the predicate itself, that one is the predicate's under this rule's earlier sentences; where no interrogative morpheme stands in the clause, there is no particle to take it and those sentences govern alone. Read the Hebrew clause for which side is the predicate rather than the English word order, since the copula stands beside the subject in every one of these; where the predicate's own words then stand apart from it, the unit is discontinuous under rule 25. **Rule 20 also governs an identifying formula where the ASV repeats one subject pronoun as both an English subject demonstrative and a predicate determiner.** Both realizations belong to that pronoun in one discontinuous unit, while the copula still goes to the written predicate: `הוּא אַהֲרֹן וּמֹשֶׁה` → *These are that Aaron and Moses* gives *These ... that* to `הוּא`, headed on *These*, and *are Aaron* to `אַהֲרֹן`. The repeated demonstrative is not `added`; it is the ASV's emphatic identifying expansion of the single pronoun.
amendments.why: The presentative sentence closed with *whether a nominal anchor or a prepositional predicate*, and two verse passes plus a recorded chapter convention read that enumeration as exhaustive, marking the *there* of `וְעוֹד חָמֵשְׁ שָׁנִים` `added` at GEN.45.6 and GEN.45.11 against the same sentence's *It is never added*. The replacement opens the anchor list, names the adverbial case, and bounds the widening by saying plainly that a cleft or impersonal *it* is not a presentative frame, which is the line this chapter draws at GEN.45.8, GEN.45.12 and GEN.45.28 and which the old wording left to be inferred. Nothing else in the rule is changed.

conventions: Supersedes the earlier GEN.45.6 entry, which was too wide. The presentative dummy “there” of a verbless clause is never `added`: it joins the unit bearing the construction-supplied copula under rule 20, whatever that unit is — in this chapter the adverb עוֹד of GEN.45.6 and GEN.45.11 (“there are yet five years”) — exactly as it joins the finite verb of GEN.45.1 (“there stood”) under rule 17 and the existential אַיִן of GEN.45.6 under rule 50. What stays `added` is a dummy rule 20 does not name: the cleft “it” of GEN.45.8 and GEN.45.12 and the impersonal “It” of GEN.45.28, for which the rule supplies the copula and nothing more.

report: Checked all 53 candidate lemma groups and read the dump end to end (the table is blind to `added` units, and two of the four findings live there). Four real problems, in GEN.45.6, .11, .16 and .27. Everything else in the table is the ASV rendering one word differently in contexts the source licenses: לְ aligned or unrepresented by whether the ASV writes a function word (rules 40, 52), אֵת unrepresented except where 'tell ... of' spends a word on the object relation (rule 16, GEN.45.13), אֶרֶץ taking 'into' only where no directive he is present (rules 32, 33), עוֹד taking the copula only where no adjectival predicate stands beside it (rule 20).

Finding 1 (GEN.45.6, GEN.45.11): the presentative dummy 'there' of a verbless clause was marked `added` in both verses, against rule 20's flat 'It is never added'. The chapter attaches the same dummy to a finite verb in GEN.45.1 ('there stood') and to the existential אַיִן in GEN.45.6 ('there shall be neither'), so the verbless clause was the odd case out rather than a licensed difference. Both now join the unit bearing the construction-supplied copula, which is עוֹד in each. The cleft and impersonal 'It' of GEN.45.8, GEN.45.12 and GEN.45.28 stay `added`: rule 20 names the presentative 'there' and otherwise covers the copula and nothing more. That line is now recorded as a convention, superseding the GEN.45.6 entry that lumped the three dummies together.

Finding 2 (GEN.45.6): בְּ + קֶרֶב -> 'hath been in' was headed on the preposition, while the chapter's four other preposition-plus-construct fusions (לִפְנֵי in GEN.45.5 and GEN.45.7, עַל פִּי in GEN.45.21, בְּטֶרֶם in GEN.45.28) are headed on the construct noun, as rule 23 directs. Source head moved to קֶרֶב.

Finding 3 (GEN.45.6): שְׁנָתַיִם -> 'two years' was headed on 'two' while the plural שָׁנִים three words later heads on 'years'. The lemma is שָׁנָה either way and the dual is grammatical number, not a different lexeme, so rule 24 puts the head on 'years' in both.

Finding 4 (GEN.45.27): 'when' in 'and when he saw the wagons' was marked `added`. Rule 55 gives a coordinator and a subordinator written together at a recast clause's left edge to the one connective morpheme, with וָאֶרְאֶה -> 'And when I looked' as its own example; the pair here is contiguous at t016-t017 and the corpus aligns a waw to 'and when' in 72 units. The waw now takes both words, headed on 'and'. The competing corpus reading heads eleven such units on 'when'; the note says so. The apodosis waw s025 stays `unrepresented` under rule 14, since the ASV opens that clause bare.

Finding 5 (GEN.45.16): the two fused experiencer units, בְּעֵינֵי פַרְעֹה -> 'Pharaoh' and בְעֵינֵי עֲבָדָיו -> 'servants', used rule 6's first-token fallback. The single English word writes one morpheme's own lexeme in each, so rules 23 and 30 supply a uniquely defensible head; source heads moved to פַרְעֹה and עֲבָדָי. The chapter heads its other fusions on the lexeme-bearing morpheme (GEN.45.5 'angry', GEN.45.20 'regard', GEN.45.21 'according to the commandment'), so these two were the outliers.

BSB: no genuine error. The R x 16 and To x 6 blocks are the documented convention difference (rules 16, 40). Spot-checked the six singletons: GEN.45.8 הָ before אֱלֹהִים has no written 'the' (rule 29); GEN.45.20 כֶם on עֵינְכֶם is absorbed by the 'regard' recasting and הוּא is the tripartite resumptive rule 20 leaves unrendered; GEN.45.22 לָ is a distributive recast with a bare object (rule 40); GEN.45.26 וְכִי writes one 'and' for the waw; GEN.45.27 s025 is the bare apodosis waw. None was changed to improve the rate.
The validator's 13 repeated notes are restatements of rules 16, 27, 29, 40 and 20, which already bind every verse, so no convention was logged for them.
GEN.45.2's five-morpheme fusion was left alone: 'wept aloud' spreads across בְּכִי and קוֹל rather than writing one morpheme's lexeme, so rule 6's fallback to the syntactic head נָתַן stands there.
